title: Poland's proposed NABE coal carve-out retires just 9 GW by 2030
programme: National Energy Security Agency (NABE) and Early Decommissioning Mechanism
problem: Poland's coal utilities have no individual total coal phase-out commitments and are expected to run coal until 2049, 19 years beyond the IEA pathway.
solution: The government proposed moving the coal plants of Enea, PGE and Tauron into a new state-owned entity, NABE, with an Early Decommissioning Mechanism buying unprofitable units for their last two years and shutting them down.
results: Of the 23 GW eligible (PGE 13 GW, Enea 5.7 GW, Tauron 4.6 GW), only 9 GW would come offline by 2030, and the plan had not yet been confirmed.
serbia_reason: Moving lignite assets out of a state utility into a public closure vehicle is an option Serbia could weigh for EPS's coal fleet. Poland's case shows a carve-out alone does not bring closure dates forward.
adapt_needed: Any carve-out of EPS lignite assets would need to be tied to binding unit closure dates.
blockers: Taking on loss-making lignite assets would put a direct burden on the Serbian state budget.
quote: An Early Decommissioning Mechanism (EDM) will be tasked with purchasing unprofitable coal assets from NABE for the last two years of their operation and gradually shutting them down. This would still only result in 9 GW of the 23 GW eligible capacity coming offline by 2030.

title: State utility PGE opens new 460 MW Turow coal unit in 2021
problem: PGE, which held 13 GW of Polish coal plants, had no coal exit date of its own unless those plants were transferred to NABE.
solution: PGE commissioned a new 460 MW coal unit, Turow B11, in 2021, extending coal generation together with the associated mine.
results: PGE was the only one of the 21 assessed utilities to add new coal capacity, and the associated mine caused substantial controversy, political tensions and serious social and economic repercussions. Wind and solar made up only 4% of PGE's capacity in 2020.
serbia_reason: Like EPS with Kostolac B3, PGE is a state-controlled utility adding a new coal unit tied to a mine. Its experience shows the controversy and lock-in such a unit creates.
adapt_needed: Not a model to copy; Serbia would need to test any new lignite unit against closure timelines and carbon costs first.
blockers: Projects that are already contracted or near completion are hard to stop.
quote: PGE even opened a new 460 MW hard coal unit, Turow B11, in 2021 and the associated mine is causing substantial controversy and political tensions along with serious social and economic repercussions. No other utility assessed for this report intends to commission new coal plants.

title: Enea's Kozienice closure schedule cuts only a third of coal by 2030
problem: Polish utility Enea operated 5.7 GW of coal plants with no commitment to a total coal phase-out.
solution: In November 2021 Enea announced unit-by-unit closure dates for Kozienice (B1-4 in 2025, B5-8 in 2027, B9-10 in 2041-2, B11 in 2048), planning to replace coal units with fossil gas.
results: The schedule removes 1.8 GW (-32%) of coal capacity by 2030 but leaves 3.9 GW running beyond the 2030 benchmark. Enea is among six utilities not compliant even with the 2040 global deadline.
serbia_reason: A unit-by-unit closure calendar is a tool Serbia could use for EPS's ageing lignite units. Enea's case shows that late dates and coal-to-gas switching limit its value.
adapt_needed: EPS closure dates would need to match the 2028 Energy Community pollution deadline, with replacement mainly by renewables rather than gas.
blockers: Without replacement capacity in place, utilities tend to push closure dates for their largest units far into the future.
quote: This equates to 1.8 GW (-32%) of capacity being removed from its coal portfolio by 2030. It will still operate 3.9 GW of coal beyond the EU/OECD benchmark of 2030.

title: ČEZ's 2038 coal exit lags Czech government's 2033 target
problem: Czechia is an advanced economy, yet coal utility ČEZ planned to burn coal well past the 2030 benchmark for such economies.
solution: ČEZ set a 2050 net zero target (excluding scope 3) and a 2038 coal exit, while the Czech government announced on 7 December 2021 a national coal exit by 2033.
results: ČEZ had not yet updated its 2038 commitment to the government's 2033 date and is listed among the significant coal laggards. Wind and solar were only 1% of its capacity in 2020.
serbia_reason: ČEZ is a state-controlled utility, like EPS, whose own coal exit lagged the government's national target. Serbia would need to align EPS's corporate plans with any national phase-out date.
adapt_needed: The state as owner would need to write a national coal exit date into EPS's business plan and investment programme.
blockers: Serbia has not announced a national coal phase-out date for EPS to align with.
quote: Based on the Czech government’s announcement on 7 December 2021 that it will phase-out coal by 2033. ČEZ has not yet updated its commitment from 2038 to 2033.

title: Bulgaria's BEH has no coal exit date and no renewables growth
programme: Bulgarian National Recovery and Resilience Plan coal phase-out (2038 or 2040)
problem: BEH, Bulgaria's state energy holding, burns coal and has neither a net zero target nor its own coal phase-out date.
solution: Bulgaria's National Recovery and Resilience Plan indicates a coal phase-out by 2038 or 2040, but BEH has made no commitment and plans no new wind or solar.
results: BEH shows little or no decrease in coal capacity from 2020 to 2030 and had 116 MW of wind and solar in 2020 with no additions planned. It did not respond to the authors' data requests.
serbia_reason: BEH is a state-owned, coal-reliant holding comparable to EPS. It shows that a national phase-out pledge achieves little when the state utility has no matching plan or renewables pipeline.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to set coal closure and renewables targets for EPS through its ownership and business planning.
blockers: State utilities can avoid transparency and targets when their government owner does not demand them.
quote: Three companies currently demonstrate no willingness to participate in the growth of the wind and solar sector by 2030: Drax, Sev.En and BEH. This is concerning since some of these utilities operate in Eastern European countries where coal phase-outs are coming fast and where leapfrogging an increase in fossil gas generation is of pronounced importance.

title: CE Oltenia had no wind or solar despite Romania's 2032 coal exit
problem: CE Oltenia, Romania's state-owned coal utility, had no coal exit date and no wind or solar capacity in 2020.
solution: Romania announced a national coal phase-out by 2032; CE Oltenia pledged 725 MW of new wind and solar by 2030 but set no coal exit date of its own.
results: CE Oltenia had not started building any wind or solar in 2020, had no net zero target and did not respond to the authors' data requests.
serbia_reason: CE Oltenia is a state-owned coal utility whose situation is close to EPS's. A national exit date without a utility renewables pipeline leaves the transition stalled.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to require EPS to build renewables, for example on mining and plant sites, alongside any closure schedule.
blockers: A coal utility's lack of capital and wind and solar expertise slows its pivot to renewables.
quote: Romania has announced that coal will be phased out by 2032. CE Oltenia has not committed to a coal phase-out date.

title: Ørsted plans ten-fold wind and solar growth and coal exit by 2023
programme: Ørsted wind expansion and asset rotation strategy
problem: Utilities must replace coal with wind and solar fast enough to meet the IEA net zero roadmap's six-fold growth by 2030.
solution: Ørsted set a 2023 coal phase-out and expands wind through asset rotation, selling newly built assets and reinvesting the profits in further wind development.
funding: Asset rotation: proceeds from selling newly built wind assets are reinvested in new projects.
results: Ørsted and EDF are the only assessed utilities adding wind and solar at an IEA NZE-compliant scale, with Ørsted growing ten-fold by 2030. Counting assets it has sold, its growth is a little more than five-fold.
serbia_reason: Ørsted is a majority state-owned utility exiting coal while building renewables at net zero pace. Its asset rotation model shows how a state utility can recycle capital into new wind and solar.
adapt_needed: EPS would need investors willing to buy stakes in operating renewables and stable rules that make such sales possible.
blockers: Serbia's smaller market and higher cost of capital may limit buyers for stakes in EPS projects.
quote: Ørsted and EDF emerge as the only utilities bringing wind and solar power to the market at an IEA NZE compliant scale. Ørsted will see a ten-fold increase and EDF almost seven-fold.
